item.content:encoded:
This is the Foundation. The goal is to contain SCPs and protect the world. Not to make them better through therapy.

And making sure the dangerous creatures that could possibly cause your brain to explode is mentally and physically healthy is pretty damn important in protecting the world.

And even if it was the goal - it failed spectacularly. Just reading the notes was painfull. The "therapeutist" is clearly aware that her subject is in distress yet she does nothing about it. She "considers" several bad options but doesn't actually do anything.

Because therapists are not omnipotent gods that can do everything on their own. The Foundation is a bureaucracy, and, like an bureaucracy, it has regulations and can't just decide the treatment for a patient that may or might not work.

Psychology may not be a hard science but it's still a science and there is ample literature to be found about curing depression.

You can't 'cure' depression. Some people are born with it. Some people naturally get it, through it being triggered by real life trauma or a chemical imbalance in the brain. Either way, it isn't something that just goes away.

We're talking about a teenage girl going through her emo phase.

emo phase

Feeling regret at killing ones own father isn't an 'emo phase'. Feeling trapped and isolated and kept away by a shadow organization is not an 'emo phase'. Being depressed isn't an 'emo phase'.

Just give her a senior male researcher to fall in love with.

Yeah, just get a strong man to fix a teenagers problems. That doesn't come across as sexist at all.1

Giving her a female doctor will automatically put her in a "motherly" position and simply make the girl "rebel against authority" even more.

Um, I'm not even sure what you're saying here, but the doctor here doesn't come across as 'motherly' in the slightest.

And she's rebelling against authority not because of an emo phase, but because she's being held in a cell against her will and being tested on.

This entire posts come across as you being completely unknowledgeable in the topics of depression, and makes you come across as a sexist when she says that she needs a man in her life that will 'love her.' Romance doesn't cure everything.

Footnotes
1. I'm not saying that being in a romantic relationship can't help people with their depression. It's just that the idea of it being a 'be all, end all' approach is just stupid.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
curing depression

This right here is the fundamental flaw in your statements. Depression is not something that can be "cured".

It is a condition with causes, however, and these causes can be addressed. Sometimes these causes are chemical imbalances, in which case I can vouch for medication's ability to patch faulty wetware and dramatically improve quality of life.

In this case, however, the causes are more complicated and harder to disrupt. Far from the mere "teenage angst" you write it off as, this is a full existential crisis: she has to bear the guilt of her father's death and knowing that she is a danger to everyone around her. She resents the fact that she is in this situation for reasons beyond her control and understanding, and resents being confined. She also resents her own feelings of resentment because point #1 means her current situation is, in fact, what is best for everyone else. As the title references, this is a viscous cycle which can only be broken by forward-thinking acceptance of her situation… or the option she ultimately chose.

As for the suggested "solution", aside from the fact that there are ethical lines that even the Foundation won't cross, there are other reasons that therapists take careful measures to avoid that sort of situation. The phrase "psychological minefield" comes to mind.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I disliked this story for a couple of reasons. TL:DR -1

+ show block
– hide block

This is the Foundation. The goal is to contain SCPs and protect the world. Not to make them better through therapy. And even if it was the goal - it failed spectacularly. Just reading the notes was painfull. The "therapeutist" is clearly aware that her subject is in distress yet she does nothing about it. She "considers" several bad options but doesn't actually do anything.

I understand that from a narrative standpoint she's here as a plot device - but usually the Foundation employees show a degree of competence that reflects the fact that the authors made the research to understand the science behind it. Psychology may not be a hard science but it's still a science and there is ample literature to be found about curing depression. I know that the popular view of modern psychology is - "we give you drugs so you can function" but (at least with good therapists) pumping you so full of drugs that you turn into a walking vegetable is the worst case scenario.

Now don't get me wrong - if the researcher in question tried every available option - and when it failed resorted to drugs - it would be much better. Also no therapist works in a vacuum. Everyone has coleagues. You have a difficult problem that you can't crack? Best solution is to get a fresh perspective - another set of eyes. Plus with Foundation you don't have to consider confidentiality issues. The SCP isn't going to sue you because you shared her personal problems with another psychologist from a different site.

And finally to address the point I mentioned at the beginning - Foundation is not trying to cure the girl but to contain the SCP. Type Green - Reality Benders are always an extreme danger no matter how strong their reality-bending is. Why not use a solution that would not be acceptable to general public but is still better than putting the girl in coma. We're talking about a teenage girl going through her emo phase. Just give her a senior male researcher to fall in love with. A strong charismatic guy with confidence, who can share plenty of interesting stories of saving the world, pay attention to her and show that he likes and cares about her. Hell give her Kondraki or Gears to fawn about. Giving her a female doctor will automatically put her in a "motherly" position and simply make the girl "rebel against authority" even more. Give her a male doctor who listens to her, doesn't treat her like a kid and doesn't ask obviously "stock psych phrases" and we've got an instant win. Is it ethical? Hell no. Will it work? Probabl yes, even if she's not interested in guys romantically. And that's just one of so many options that could be attempted. I could write about it for days but there are books already written about curing depression and teenage angst. Just go read any one of them.

In conclusion there are tons of solutions and since I belive the Foundation to be composed of the "best of the best" or at least professionals in any given field - I'd expect the researcher to show at least a basic amount of skill above a first-year lab assistant. Or for the story to end with the researcher being reassigned to D-class for utter incompetence. Possibly along with the HR who hired her.

item.content:encoded:
Well that was a good read and a little moving at the end so upvoted for that…

… but it doesn't seem to mesh well with 055. 055's containment is much more elaborate for starters. I think there is a big difference between a reality bender and a self-keeping secret.

You could say that 055 could be a perfect all-powerful reality bender limited to affecting knowledge of itself, but Marissa isn't quite that. Her abilities are random. You could say that her final act of self-deletion was effectually removing knowledge of herself, but she only did that once, whereas my impression is that 055 does so constantly. 055 still exists. It's definitely there, it's definitely something. If Marissa erased herself, she wouldn't be an SCP.

I saw that ending coming, but I thought you would have made her destroy the site and those around her in rage. I was wrong. This was better. Well done.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Oh man, that reveal got me good. I knew the use of her name and non-mention of her number had to be significant, but for some reason I never manage to guess when a tale is about 055. It's like I just keep forgetting it exists…

Anyway, I really like this. Good (if anger-inducing on a very personal level) portrayal of how these things often work: of course she's angry, of course she's miserable, can't the so-called therapists do more than state the obvious external consequences of what they do to her and why? Abilities she can't control, that have negative impacts on her life to begin with, and then the Foundation gets its hands on her. Honestly, in my view, she got a happy ending.

I love reading about this universe. I wouldn't want to be part of it. This is why. +1
